## Purpose

Reduce DSpark draft latency with opt-in candidate pruning of the Markov projection. At each position, candidates are the union of the top-k backbone logits and the top-m precomputed Markov-bias entries. The sequential walk evaluates and samples within that union. `markov_topk=0` keeps the full-vocabulary path.

This changes the draft proposal distribution. Correct probabilistic rejection sampling must use exactly the truncated distribution used to draw the draft tokens; draft quality and acceptance length can change. Target-distribution preservation therefore depends on sampler/cache correctness and is not established by throughput measurements alone.

## Implementation and compatibility

- Use a fused Triton walk over base-logit and optional static Markov candidates.
- Cache the candidate proposal logits for probabilistic rejection sampling.
- Preserve draft-to-target vocabulary mapping.
- Keep pruning disabled by default; unsupported quantized or sharded Markov heads use the dense path.

- Use the existing platform-aware top-k dispatcher so importing DSpark does not unconditionally require FlashInfer.
- Use the maximum score for overlapping candidate IDs, matching token-keyed Gumbel sampling; synchronize cache clearing before updates.
- Fall back to dense drafting when online acceptance estimation or draft watermarking is enabled. Trained confidence heads remain supported.
- Exclude padded W2 rows before building static candidates.
- Narrow the optional speculative config before resolving the candidate budget.
- Extend the existing DSpark test suites for greedy chains, probabilistic sampling/cache agreement, reduced vocabularies, CUDA graph cache reuse, static-candidate construction, and dense fallbacks.

Platform-aware top-k uses deterministic sorted selection. GPU correctness, accuracy, and performance validation of the final implementation remain outstanding.

## Prior benchmark results

The author previously reported throughput measurements on 8 Hopper GPUs with Qwen3-4B. For base top-k=32 and Markov top-m=32, the reported improvements were approximately 5.51% on C-Eval, 4.99% on GSM8K, 5.18% on Math500, 6.41% on HumanEval, and 5.86% on MBPP. The later SPEED measurements at temperature=0 reported 4.2% on 16K and 5.3% on 8K.

These are historical measurements from before the correctness and compatibility fixes described above. Gains are configuration-dependent: some settings regress, so this PR does not claim a speedup for every top-k/top-m combination. The existing tables report throughput and acceptance metrics, not task accuracy.

Original result images:

![C-Eval](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9a6729ac-4399-49a6-9bb3-def753557724)
![GSM8K](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/de15a955-f33b-4c82-810a-c4bf51d3f9ed)
![Math500](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/bc3ba2d3-1616-4658-a684-c50015a52f4c)
![HumanEval](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/630ff36a-b680-47ec-a9ed-91b25dcbace8)
![MBPP](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6cc52259-6f51-4146-b366-cb336c326a1f)

[SPEED benchmark response](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56694#issuecomment-5756387074)

Original serving configuration:

```bash
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-4B \
  --no-enable-flashinfer-autotune \
  --max-num-seqs 128 \
  --data-parallel-size 8 \
  --no-enable-prefix-caching \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","model":"/personal/checkpoints/speculators/dspark_qwen3_4b","num_speculative_tokens":8,"markov_topk":16,"markov_bias_topk":16}'

vllm bench serve \
  --base-url http://localhost:8000 \
  --model Qwen/Qwen3-4B \
  --dataset-name custom \
  --dataset-path /personal/data/ceval/ceval-1040-prompt.jsonl \
  --num-prompts 1040 --temperature 0 --custom-output-len 3072 \
  --no-oversample --max-concurrency 32
```

The published checkpoint is https://huggingface.co/AQ-MedAI/Qwen3-4B-DSpark. The command above uses the original author's local paths; it is not a newly executed benchmark.

## Validation

- PASS: Ruff 0.14.0 checks and formatting for the six PR source files plus both extended test files.
- PASS: mypy 1.20.2 / Python 3.12 through `tools/pre_commit/mypy.py`, in an isolated environment with the same dependencies as the pre-commit hook.
- PASS: local SPDX, lazy-import, forbidden-import, torch.cuda API, config-docstring/default, and boolean-context-manager checks.
- PASS: standalone CPU smoke check of the actual `compute_markov_bias_top_ids` implementation against dense top-k, for scale=1 and scale=-1. This is not a full pytest run.
- PASS: `git diff --check`.
- NOT COMPLETED: full pre-commit; GitHub hook dependency initialization stalled and was interrupted.
- BLOCKED AT COLLECTION: `.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dspark_topk.py tests/v1/worker/test_dspark_utils.py -q`; the macOS environment is not a complete vLLM installation (last missing module: uvloop; native vLLM extension and Triton also unavailable).
- NOT RUN: GPU kernel tests, compute-sanitizer, end-to-end accuracy evaluation, and post-fix throughput benchmarks. No Linux GPU environment is currently available.

Lint and type-check commands (the eight files are the six PR source files plus the two extended test files):

```bash
files=(
  vllm/config/speculative.py
  vllm/model_executor/models/qwen3_dspark.py
  vllm/transformers_utils/configs/speculators/algos.py
  vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py
  vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/dspark/speculator.py
  vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/dspark/topk_markov.py
  tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dspark_topk.py
  tests/v1/worker/test_dspark_utils.py
)
.venv/bin/ruff check "${files[@]}"
.venv/bin/ruff format --check "${files[@]}"
# Isolated environment with the pre-commit hook's pinned mypy and dependencies:
PATH="/tmp/vllm-pr56694-mypy/.venv/bin:$PATH" \
  /tmp/vllm-pr56694-mypy/.venv/bin/python \
  tools/pre_commit/mypy.py 3.12 "${files[@]}"
git diff --check
```

Before merging, run the extended pytest suites on Linux GPU, check the duplicate-candidate/cache-reuse kernels with compute-sanitizer, and compare accuracy and throughput against the dense DSpark path on the same checkpoint and workloads.

## Relationship to existing work and AI assistance

This updates the existing PR rather than opening a duplicate. #57770 optimizes full-vocabulary greedy selection; #61869 focuses on the specialized DSv4.1 dense Markov loop and post-forward graph. This PR instead prunes the candidate set used by the vanilla DSpark Markov projection.

OpenAI Codex assisted with the review, code changes, tests, and this description. The submitting human has reviewed the changes and authorized their submission. Relevant GPU tests and model evaluations still need to be run; the results above do not claim those checks passed.

@benchislett @MatthewBonanni Could you please review this DSpark optimization?

This PR adds opt-in, training-free Markov candidate pruning: combine the top-k backbone logits with the top-m Markov-bias candidates, then run a fused Triton walk over their union instead of the full vocabulary. The goal is to reduce W2 projection work and memory traffic while retaining tokens favored by the Markov transition; pruning by backbone logits alone can reduce acceptance. The proposal cache matches the pruned sampling distribution for rejection sampling, with dense fallbacks for unsupported combinations.

The green entries in the existing Qwen3-4B benchmark tables (8 Hopper GPUs, base top-k=32 + Markov bias top-k=32, versus dense DSpark) show:

| Dataset | Output throughput gain |
| --- | ---: |
| C-Eval | +5.51% |
| GSM8K | +4.99% |
| Math500 | +5.18% |
| HumanEval | +6.41% |
| MBPP | +5.86% |

These are the measurements already attached to this PR; acceptance length stays close to the baseline in those tables. Feedback on candidate selection, proposal-cache/rejection-sampling consistency, and fallback behavior would be especially helpful. Thank you!

Hi @mugglewei97! 

The throughput improvement of the PR looks promising. Perhaps there are also latency improvements besides that. However, the choice of concurrency + data parallelism + 4B model is odd. If running 4B then a single GPU should be fine. If you have access to many GPUs, a larger model would also be informative. It would be great if you can benchmark at several concurrency levels, e.g. c=1, 8, 64 and report total throughput and TPOT.

The footprint of this PR is pretty large and you introduce several changes. There is scope to simplify. As far as I understand, you:
* replace `dspark_draft_topk`, which might not be necessary.
* introduce `markov_bias_topk`, which is genuinely novel
* introduce a triton kernel to fuse the sequential sampling, removing the looping
* pre-compute markov bias values

The DSpark code path is very important, and we would like to avoid introducing risky changes. It means that if you can minimize your changes, they are more likely to land. Some ideas here:
* Reuse `dspark_draft_topk` for the both candidate sets. Your suggested config takes the value 32 for both anyway.
* Adding `markov_bias_topk` almost restores the AL of full DSpark. Is this perhaps already driving most of the gains? Perhaps we can drop all other optimizations.
* Fusing the loop with Triton seems sensible, but not strictly needed. How much improvement does this actually drive?
* Same for pre-computation

Thanks @tomasruizt and @benchislett. In 1d1bbc9, I reduced the PR to three files and reused `dspark_draft_topk` for both candidate sets. @mugglewei97 My agent was able to reproduce the AL almost matching full-vocab, but not any statistically significant speedups over full-vocab.

<details>
<summary>Validation setup, measurements and limitations</summary>

Measurements were collected on November 2, 2026, against `f94d7ff8ae9ab663e4e8b08f9dd0f0326bad0b16` (the PR head tested that day). This tests the current simplified implementation, rather than reproducing the historical DP8, 3072-output-cap experiments. The author also [noted that the older performance results do not apply to the simplified revision](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56694#issuecomment-6271811409).

**Setup and controls**

- One NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3, TP=1 and DP=1. All included performance comparisons use the same healthy GPU, with median SM clock 1980MHz and maximum recorded temperature 62°C.
- Target: `Qwen/Qwen3-4B`, revision `1cfa9a7208912126459214e8b04321603b3df60c`.
- Draft: `AQ-MedAI/Qwen3-4B-DSpark`, revision `49d6beedccdb7e2500382171461cb9868c2c5fbc`, with eight speculative tokens.
- AIPerf 0.13.0, Python 3.12 and PyTorch 2.14.0+cu130. The Python source was the pinned PR archive. All modes used identical precompiled extensions from `759d13479` (the October 30 runtime environment).
- SPEED-Bench 8K and 16K throughput buckets, fully reconstructed with NVIDIA's loader, including the masked source-data entries. Temperature 0, natural EOS, output cap 1024, thinking disabled and prefix caching disabled.
- Three 30-second AIPerf trials per workload/concurrency/mode, with up to 180 seconds to drain outstanding requests. Eight 512-token output-check requests ran outside the timed measurements before each mode.
- Full-vocabulary DSpark: PR source with `dspark_draft_topk` unset.
- Base-only top-32: the same source tree with only `speculator.py` restored from `1cb31be7028457c7eae7b6fabca1941d5d3c4730` (the upstream base used for this validation), with `dspark_draft_topk=32`.
- PR union: unchanged PR implementation with `dspark_draft_topk=32`, selecting the union of 32 base-logit and 32 Markov-bias candidates.

There are 48 included trials: 18 full-vocabulary, 18 PR union and 12 base-only control trials. The base-only control covered c=1/8, while full-vocabulary and PR union covered c=1/4/8. They completed 1,906 requests with zero errors, cancellations or preemptions. These are request completions across repeated workloads, not 1,906 independent prompts. The minimum steady window was 19.57 seconds.

Three c=64 pilots were excluded because of KV-cache preemptions and steady windows of only 0.73–1.97 seconds. Five trials from an attempted second-GPU comparison were also excluded because that GPU reached 91°C and 345MHz. Its replacement measurements used the healthy GPU.

**Throughput and TPOT**

Values below are medians across the three trials. Percentage changes are ratios of medians, PR versus full-vocabulary DSpark. Throughput is output tok/s. A positive TPOT change means higher latency.

| Workload | c | Full-vocab steady tok/s | PR steady tok/s | Steady throughput change | AIPerf whole-run throughput change | Full-vocab TPOT (ms) | PR TPOT (ms) | TPOT change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 8K | 1 | 536.3 | 541.5 | +0.98% | +0.93% | 1.641 | 1.619 | -1.33% |
| 8K | 4 | 1462.5 | 1466.4 | +0.27% | +3.32% | 2.462 | 2.465 | +0.15% |
| 8K | 8 | 1832.5 | 1886.7 | +2.96% | +2.84% | 3.786 | 3.758 | -0.75% |
| 16K | 1 | 492.7 | 495.7 | +0.62% | +0.89% | 1.795 | 1.775 | -1.16% |
| 16K | 4 | 936.6 | 944.7 | +0.86% | -0.33% | 3.553 | 3.614 | +1.73% |
| 16K | 8 | 1122.1 | 1134.5 | +1.10% | +2.00% | 6.297 | 6.061 | -3.75% |

The steady window starts at the c-th request completion and ends at the last request submission. Tokens inside that window are estimated from stream timestamps by spreading each request's total output tokens uniformly across its streamed chunks. TPOT averages requests starting inside the steady window. AIPerf's whole-run throughput is also shown to expose the sensitivity to window and drain effects.

The PR's median steady throughput relative to the existing base-only top-32 control was +8.27%/+2.99% on 8K c=1/8 and +2.67%/+1.40% on 16K c=1/8. These comparisons have the same statistical and workload-composition limitations as the full-vocabulary comparisons.

**Statistical limits**

No statistically significant speedup is established. An exploratory two-sided exact label-permutation diagnostic, using the absolute log ratio of medians and all 20 allocations of three versus three trials, gives the following p-values:

| Workload | c | Steady throughput p | AIPerf whole-run throughput p |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 8K | 1 | 0.6 | 0.6 |
| 8K | 4 | 1.0 | 0.4 |
| 8K | 8 | 0.4 | 0.4 |
| 16K | 1 | 0.4 | 0.2 |
| 16K | 4 | 1.0 | 1.0 |
| 16K | 8 | 0.4 | 0.2 |

These are exploratory diagnostics, not confirmatory tests. Modes ran in sequential blocks, with one server startup per mode within each sweep. The three repeats therefore do not measure startup-to-startup variation, the blocks do not justify exchangeability, and duration-bounded runs consume different prompt prefixes. Several observed ranges overlap. A stronger speedup claim needs matched workloads and randomized, interleaved comparisons across independent startups.

**Acceptance length**

The strongest available comparisons use c=1 runs with matching ordered prompt sequences and identical per-request output-length vectors:

| Workload | Matched requests | Base-only AL | PR AL | Full-vocab AL | PR vs base-only | PR vs full-vocab |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 8K | 17 | 3.5631 | 3.6556 | 3.6598 | +2.60% | -0.11% |
| 16K | 15 | 3.6840 | 3.7108 | 3.7206 | +0.73% | -0.26% |

This supports AL recovery relative to base-only pruning on the sampled prompts, with the PR remaining slightly below full-vocabulary DSpark. The matched 8K subset contains one PR repeat, one full-vocab repeat and three base-only repeats. The matched 16K subset contains two PR repeats and three repeats for each control, reusing the same prompts. With only 15–17 distinct prompts, this does not establish statistical significance or generalization of the AL effect. Draft steps within a request are correlated and cannot be treated as independent prompt samples.

For completeness, the medians across all timed trials are:

| Workload | c | Base-only AL | PR AL | Full-vocab AL | PR vs full-vocab |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 8K | 1 | 3.5631 | 3.7133 | 3.7173 | -0.11% |
| 8K | 4 | n/a | 3.6313 | 3.6002 | +0.86% |
| 8K | 8 | 3.3160 | 3.4543 | 3.3869 | +1.99% |
| 16K | 1 | 3.6840 | 3.7108 | 3.7206 | -0.26% |
| 16K | 4 | n/a | 3.3768 | 3.3940 | -0.51% |
| 16K | 8 | 3.3740 | 3.3541 | 3.3251 | +0.87% |

These all-run medians should not be interpreted as matched-prompt AL improvements. For example, the 8K c=1 PR median covers 19 requests while the base-only runs cover 17. The higher-concurrency comparisons use different prompt sequences. There is no consistent demonstrated AL improvement over full-vocabulary DSpark.

The counter audit passes for all 48 included runs: `AL = 1 + accepted_tokens / num_drafts` recomputes exactly, all 384 per-position counters are complete, bounded and monotone, and their sums equal accepted-token totals. Every run records eight proposed tokens per draft. Server generation-token deltas equal client output-token totals in every run, and scrape ranges bracket the profiling phases. AL covers the whole profiling cell, including drain, rather than only the steady throughput window.

**Targeted correctness checks**

All 18 targeted tests passed, including candidate selection, reduced-vocabulary mapping and probabilistic proposal-cache agreement after CUDA graph replay. The test fixture initialized `draft_logits_num_shards=1` and `draft_logits_shard_idx=0`. Production PR code was unchanged.

End-to-end losslessness remains unverified. The eight-prompt greedy output check was inconclusive: PR versus full-vocab agreed on 5/8 and 3/8 prompts in the two sweeps, while a second full-vocab startup agreed with the first on only 4/8. [The pinned vLLM reproducibility documentation](https://github.com/mugglewei97/vllm/blob/f94d7ff8ae9ab663e4e8b08f9dd0f0326bad0b16/docs/usage/reproducibility.md) notes that default online serving does not guarantee reproducible outputs. Batch invariance was disabled for these performance measurements.

**Reproduction settings**

Use a writable shared model cache and the pinned model revisions:

```bash
export HF_HUB_CACHE=/path/to/writable/shared/cache
hf download Qwen/Qwen3-4B \
  --revision 1cfa9a7208912126459214e8b04321603b3df60c \
  --cache-dir "$HF_HUB_CACHE"
hf download AQ-MedAI/Qwen3-4B-DSpark \
  --revision 49d6beedccdb7e2500382171461cb9868c2c5fbc \
  --cache-dir "$HF_HUB_CACHE"
export TARGET=$HF_HUB_CACHE/models--Qwen--Qwen3-4B/snapshots/1cfa9a7208912126459214e8b04321603b3df60c
DRAFT=$HF_HUB_CACHE/models--AQ-MedAI--Qwen3-4B-DSpark/snapshots/49d6beedccdb7e2500382171461cb9868c2c5fbc

# Full-vocabulary DSpark
SPEC='{"method":"dspark","model":"'"$DRAFT"'","num_speculative_tokens":8}'

# PR union, or base-only with the upstream speculator.py control described above
SPEC='{"method":"dspark","model":"'"$DRAFT"'","num_speculative_tokens":8,"dspark_draft_topk":32}'

VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1 vllm serve "$TARGET" \
  --served-model-name qwen --max-model-len 32768 \
  --max-num-seqs 128 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
  --no-enable-prefix-caching --disable-uvicorn-access-log \
  --no-enable-flashinfer-autotune --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8664 --speculative-config "$SPEC"
```

The dataset revision was `nvidia/SPEED-Bench@fbd6dc64353a3153bf24252a113ebd6d2cff9dec`. ## Purpose

Reduce DSpark draft latency with opt-in candidate pruning of the Markov projection. At each position, candidates are the union of the top-k backbone logits and the top-m precomputed Markov-bias entries. The sequential walk evaluates and samples within that union. `markov_topk=0` keeps the full-vocabulary path.

This changes the draft proposal distribution. Correct probabilistic rejection sampling must use exactly the truncated distribution used to draw the draft tokens; draft quality and acceptance length can change. Target-distribution preservation therefore depends on sampler/cache correctness and is not established by throughput measurements alone.

## Implementation and compatibility

- Use a fused Triton walk over base-logit and optional static Markov candidates.
- Cache the candidate proposal logits for probabilistic rejection sampling.
- Preserve draft-to-target vocabulary mapping.
- Keep pruning disabled by default; unsupported quantized or sharded Markov heads use the dense path.

- Use the existing platform-aware top-k dispatcher so importing DSpark does not unconditionally require FlashInfer.
- Use the maximum score for overlapping candidate IDs, matching token-keyed Gumbel sampling; synchronize cache clearing before updates.
- Fall back to dense drafting when online acceptance estimation or draft watermarking is enabled. Trained confidence heads remain supported.
- Exclude padded W2 rows before building static candidates.
- Narrow the optional speculative config before resolving the candidate budget.
- Extend the existing DSpark test suites for greedy chains, probabilistic sampling/cache agreement, reduced vocabularies, CUDA graph cache reuse, static-candidate construction, and dense fallbacks.

Platform-aware top-k uses deterministic sorted selection. GPU correctness, accuracy, and performance validation of the final implementation remain outstanding.

## Prior benchmark results

The author previously reported throughput measurements on 8 Hopper GPUs with Qwen3-4B. For base top-k=32 and Markov top-m=32, the reported improvements were approximately 5.51% on C-Eval, 4.99% on GSM8K, 5.18% on Math500, 6.41% on HumanEval, and 5.86% on MBPP. The later SPEED measurements at temperature=0 reported 4.2% on 16K and 5.3% on 8K.

These are historical measurements from before the correctness and compatibility fixes described above. Gains are configuration-dependent: some settings regress, so this PR does not claim a speedup for every top-k/top-m combination. The existing tables report throughput and acceptance metrics, not task accuracy.

```bash
  --no-enable-flashinfer-autotune \
  --max-num-seqs 128 \
  --data-parallel-size 8 \

  --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","model":"/personal/checkpoints/speculators/dspark_qwen3_4b","num_speculative_tokens":8,"markov_topk":16,"markov_bias_topk":16}'

  --dataset-path /personal/data/ceval/ceval-1040-prompt.jsonl \
  --num-prompts 1040 --temperature 0 --custom-output-len 3072 \

```

The published checkpoint is https://huggingface.co/AQ-MedAI/Qwen3-4B-DSpark. The command above uses the original author's local paths; it is not a newly executed benchmark.

- PASS: standalone CPU smoke check of the actual `compute_markov_bias_top_ids` implementation against dense top-k, for scale=1 and scale=-1. This is not a full pytest run.
- PASS: `git diff --check`.
- NOT COMPLETED: full pre-commit; GitHub hook dependency initialization stalled and was interrupted.
- BLOCKED AT COLLECTION: `.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dspark_topk.py tests/v1/worker/test_dspark_utils.py -q`; the macOS environment is not a complete vLLM installation (last missing module: uvloop; native vLLM extension and Triton also unavailable).
- NOT RUN: GPU kernel tests, compute-sanitizer, end-to-end accuracy evaluation, and post-fix throughput benchmarks. No Linux GPU environment is currently available.

## Relationship to existing work and AI assistance

This updates the existing PR rather than opening a duplicate. #57770 optimizes full-vocabulary greedy selection; #61869 focuses on the specialized DSv4.1 dense Markov loop and post-forward graph. This PR instead prunes the candidate set used by the vanilla DSpark Markov projection.

+"""Greedy candidate-pruned Markov sampling, fused across draft positions."""
+
+import torch
+
+from vllm.triton_utils import tl, triton
+
+
+@triton.jit
+def _markov_walk_kernel(
+    logits_ptr,
+    base_values_ptr,
+    base_ids_ptr,
+    markov_ids_ptr,
+    markov_biases_ptr,
+    w1_ptr,
+    w2_ptr,
+    input_ids_ptr,
+    anchors_ptr,
+    output_ptr,
+    d2t_ptr,
+    logits_req_stride: tl.constexpr,
+    logits_step_stride: tl.constexpr,
+    w1_stride: tl.constexpr,
+    w2_stride: tl.constexpr,
+    output_stride: tl.constexpr,
+    SCALE: tl.constexpr,
+    VOCAB: tl.constexpr,
+    STEPS: tl.constexpr,
+    K: tl.constexpr,
+    RANK: tl.constexpr,
+    BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr,
+    BLOCK_R: tl.constexpr,
+    HAS_D2T: tl.constexpr,
+):
+    req = tl.program_id(0).to(tl.int64)
+    cols = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_K)
+    valid = cols < K
+    prev = tl.load(input_ids_ptr + tl.load(anchors_ptr + req)).to(tl.int64)
+
+    for step in range(STEPS):
+        base_offset = (req * STEPS + step) * K + cols
+        base_ids = tl.load(base_ids_ptr + base_offset, valid, other=0).to(tl.int64)
+        bias_ids = tl.load(markov_ids_ptr + prev * K + cols, valid, other=0).to(
+            tl.int64
+        )
+        # The cached score overwrites the online score for overlapping IDs.
+        overlap = (
+            tl.sum(
+                ((base_ids[:, None] == bias_ids[None, :]) & valid[None, :]).to(
+                    tl.int32
+                ),
+                axis=1,
+            )
+            > 0
+        )
+        base_valid = valid & ~overlap
+        correction = tl.full((BLOCK_K,), 0, tl.float32)
+        for start in range(0, RANK, BLOCK_R):
+            ranks = start + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_R)
+            embed = tl.load(w1_ptr + prev * w1_stride + ranks, ranks < RANK, 0).to(
+                tl.float32
+            )
+            weight = tl.load(
+                w2_ptr + base_ids[:, None] * w2_stride + ranks[None, :],
+                base_valid[:, None] & (ranks[None, :] < RANK),
+                other=0,
+            ).to(tl.float32)
+            correction += tl.sum(weight * embed[None, :], axis=1)
+        base = tl.load(base_values_ptr + base_offset, valid, other=0).to(tl.float32)
+        base_scores = (base + correction * SCALE).to(logits_ptr.dtype.element_ty)
+        bias_base = tl.load(
+            logits_ptr + req * logits_req_stride + step * logits_step_stride + bias_ids,
+            valid,
+            other=0,
+        ).to(tl.float32)
+        bias = tl.load(markov_biases_ptr + prev * K + cols, valid, other=0).to(
+            tl.float32
+        )
+        bias_scores = (bias_base + bias).to(logits_ptr.dtype.element_ty)
+        scores = tl.cat(
+            tl.where(base_valid, base_scores.to(tl.float32), -float("inf")),
+            tl.where(valid, bias_scores.to(tl.float32), -float("inf")),
+        )
+        ids = tl.cat(base_ids, bias_ids)
+        # Dense argmax selects the first NaN, otherwise the lowest ID at a tie.
+        nan_ids = tl.min(tl.where(scores != scores, ids, VOCAB), axis=0)
+        maximum = tl.max(tl.where(scores != scores, -float("inf"), scores), axis=0)
+        token = tl.min(tl.where(scores == maximum, ids, VOCAB), axis=0)
+        token = tl.where(maximum == -float("inf"), 0, token)
+        token = tl.where(nan_ids < VOCAB, nan_ids, token)
+        if HAS_D2T:
+            token += tl.load(d2t_ptr + token)
+        tl.store(output_ptr + req * output_stride + step, token)
+        prev = token
+

+def markov_walk_topk(
+    *,
+    base_logits: torch.Tensor,
+    base_values: torch.Tensor,
+    base_ids: torch.Tensor,
+    markov_ids: torch.Tensor,
+    markov_biases: torch.Tensor,
+    w1: torch.Tensor,
+    w2: torch.Tensor,
+    input_ids: torch.Tensor,
+    anchor_indices: torch.Tensor,
+    draft_tokens: torch.Tensor,
+    d2t: torch.Tensor | None,
+    scale: float,
+) -> None:
+    """Write a greedy chain with one program per request.
+
+    Base logits are [batch, steps, vocab] with contiguous vocabulary rows;
+    top-k values/IDs are contiguous [batch, steps, k]. Cached Markov values/IDs
+    are contiguous [target_vocab, k]. Weights are unquantized, row-contiguous
+    [vocab, rank]; d2t holds optional draft-to-target ID offsets. FP32 reduction
+    can round differently from the unfused matrix multiplication.
+    """
+    batch, steps, k = base_ids.shape
+    rank = w1.shape[1]
+    _markov_walk_kernel[(batch,)](
+        base_logits,
+        base_values,
+        base_ids,
+        markov_ids,
+        markov_biases,
+        w1,
+        w2,
+        input_ids,
+        anchor_indices,
+        draft_tokens,
+        d2t,
+        base_logits.stride(0),
+        base_logits.stride(1),
+        w1.stride(0),
+        w2.stride(0),
+        draft_tokens.stride(0),
+        scale,
+        base_logits.shape[-1],
+        steps,
+        k,
+        rank,
+        triton.next_power_of_2(k),
+        min(triton.next_power_of_2(rank), 64),
+        d2t is not None,
+        num_warps=4,
+        enable_fp_fusion=False,
+    )

Hi @tomasruizt, glad to update some info

**Q1: "Reuse dspark_draft_topk for both candidate sets"**
Already done. The current PR uses a single dspark_draft_topk=32 to control both the base top-k and the Markov top-k. There is no separate markov_bias_topk parameter.

**Q2: "Adding markov top-k almost restores the AL of full DSpark. Is this already driving most of the gains? Perhaps we can drop all other optimizations."**
Yes. Markov candidates are the primary source of gain. On our GSM8K benchmark with Qwen3-4B at c=8:

| dense, full vocab     | 3.59   |              
| base-only k=32       | 3.11    | −0.48          
| base+Markov k=32 | 3.55   | −0.04          

Markov candidates recover 0.44/0.48 = 91.7% of the AL lost to top-k truncation. Also, GSM8K dense full vocab accept len is 5.96, and base+Markov k=32 accept len is 5.94

This suggests most of the gap comes from missing good candidates that the Markov bias can identify, and the remaining optimizations (Triton fusion, separate proposal cache, separate config) are not necessary.

The current PR has already dropped all other optimizations, keeping only the precomputed candidate ID table. The C-online ablation confirms  switching to online computation yields identical acceptance rates (31.6%), so the quality gain is from Markov candidates themselves, not from  precomputation.

**Q3: "Fusing the loop with Triton — how much improvement does this actually drive?"**
Not included and not needed. The Python for loop overhead (~0.8 ms per step for 8 iterations) is hidden by CUDA async dispatch, not worth the complexity of a custom Triton kernel.


**Q4: "Same for pre-computation — how much does it actually drive?"**
Precomputation does not affect correctness, only speed. 
Ablation results:

│ precomputed table       │ 737 tok/s │ 4151 tok/s  │ 31.6%           
│ compute online             │ 666 tok/s │ 4016 tok/s │ 31.6%           

Precomputation saves 9.7% at c=1 and 3.2% at c=64.
Cost: the table is vocab_size × k × 8 = 151,936 × 32 × 8 ≈ 37 MB of GPU memory. Runtime GPU memory usage is unchanged. First startup incurs ~20 s to build the table; subsequent starts have no extra overhead.
Conclusion: precomputation is worth keeping. A 9.7% speedup for 37 MB of memory is a good trade-off.

@benchislett @MatthewBonanni Could you please review this DSpark optimization?

This PR adds opt-in, training-free Markov candidate pruning: combine the top-k backbone logits with the top-m Markov-bias candidates, then run a fused Triton walk over their union instead of the full vocabulary. The goal is to reduce W2 projection work and memory traffic while retaining tokens favored by the Markov transition; pruning by backbone logits alone can reduce acceptance. The proposal cache matches the pruned sampling distribution for rejection sampling, with dense fallbacks for unsupported combinations.

The green entries in the existing Qwen3-4B benchmark tables (8 Hopper GPUs, base top-k=32 + Markov bias top-k=32, versus dense DSpark) show:

| Dataset | Output throughput gain |
| --- | ---: |

Hi @mugglewei97! 

The throughput improvement of the PR looks promising. Perhaps there are also latency improvements besides that. However, the choice of concurrency + data parallelism + 4B model is odd. If running 4B then a single GPU should be fine. If you have access to many GPUs, a larger model would also be informative. It would be great if you can benchmark at several concurrency levels, e.g. c=1, 8, 64 and report total throughput and TPOT.

The footprint of this PR is pretty large and you introduce several changes. There is scope to simplify. As far as I understand, you:
* replace `dspark_draft_topk`, which might not be necessary.
* introduce `markov_bias_topk`, which is genuinely novel
* introduce a triton kernel to fuse the sequential sampling, removing the looping
* pre-compute markov bias values

The DSpark code path is very important, and we would like to avoid introducing risky changes. It means that if you can minimize your changes, they are more likely to land. Some ideas here:
* Reuse `dspark_draft_topk` for the both candidate sets. Your suggested config takes the value 32 for both anyway.
* Adding `markov_bias_topk` almost restores the AL of full DSpark. Is this perhaps already driving most of the gains? Perhaps we can drop all other optimizations.
* Fusing the loop with Triton seems sensible, but not strictly needed. How much improvement does this actually drive?
* Same for pre-computation

@mugglewei97 My agent was able to reproduce the AL almost matching full-vocab, but not any statistically significant speedups over full-vocab.

<details>
<summary>Validation setup, measurements and limitations</summary>

Measurements were collected on November 2, 2026, against `f94d7ff8ae9ab663e4e8b08f9dd0f0326bad0b16` (the PR head tested that day). This tests the current simplified implementation, rather than reproducing the historical DP8, 3072-output-cap experiments. The author also [noted that the older performance results do not apply to the simplified revision](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56694#issuecomment-6271811409).

**Setup and controls**

- One NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3, TP=1 and DP=1. All included performance comparisons use the same healthy GPU, with median SM clock 1980MHz and maximum recorded temperature 62°C.
- Target: `Qwen/Qwen3-4B`, revision `1cfa9a7208912126459214e8b04321603b3df60c`.
- Draft: `AQ-MedAI/Qwen3-4B-DSpark`, revision `49d6beedccdb7e2500382171461cb9868c2c5fbc`, with eight speculative tokens.
- AIPerf 0.13.0, Python 3.12 and PyTorch 2.14.0+cu130. The Python source was the pinned PR archive. All modes used identical precompiled extensions from `759d13479` (the October 30 runtime environment).
- SPEED-Bench 8K and 16K throughput buckets, fully reconstructed with NVIDIA's loader, including the masked source-data entries. Temperature 0, natural EOS, output cap 1024, thinking disabled and prefix caching disabled.
- Three 30-second AIPerf trials per workload/concurrency/mode, with up to 180 seconds to drain outstanding requests. Eight 512-token output-check requests ran outside the timed measurements before each mode.
- Full-vocabulary DSpark: PR source with `dspark_draft_topk` unset.
- Base-only top-32: the same source tree with only `speculator.py` restored from `1cb31be7028457c7eae7b6fabca1941d5d3c4730` (the upstream base used for this validation), with `dspark_draft_topk=32`.
- PR union: unchanged PR implementation with `dspark_draft_topk=32`, selecting the union of 32 base-logit and 32 Markov-bias candidates.

There are 48 included trials: 18 full-vocabulary, 18 PR union and 12 base-only control trials. The base-only control covered c=1/8, while full-vocabulary and PR union covered c=1/4/8. They completed 1,906 requests with zero errors, cancellations or preemptions. These are request completions across repeated workloads, not 1,906 independent prompts. The minimum steady window was 19.57 seconds.

Three c=64 pilots were excluded because of KV-cache preemptions and steady windows of only 0.73–1.97 seconds. Five trials from an attempted second-GPU comparison were also excluded because that GPU reached 91°C and 345MHz. Its replacement measurements used the healthy GPU.

**Throughput and TPOT**

Values below are medians across the three trials. Percentage changes are ratios of medians, PR versus full-vocabulary DSpark. Throughput is output tok/s. A positive TPOT change means higher latency.

| Workload | c | Full-vocab steady tok/s | PR steady tok/s | Steady throughput change | AIPerf whole-run throughput change | Full-vocab TPOT (ms) | PR TPOT (ms) | TPOT change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 8K | 1 | 536.3 | 541.5 | +0.98% | +0.93% | 1.641 | 1.619 | -1.33% |
| 8K | 4 | 1462.5 | 1466.4 | +0.27% | +3.32% | 2.462 | 2.465 | +0.15% |
| 8K | 8 | 1832.5 | 1886.7 | +2.96% | +2.84% | 3.786 | 3.758 | -0.75% |
| 16K | 1 | 492.7 | 495.7 | +0.62% | +0.89% | 1.795 | 1.775 | -1.16% |
| 16K | 4 | 936.6 | 944.7 | +0.86% | -0.33% | 3.553 | 3.614 | +1.73% |
| 16K | 8 | 1122.1 | 1134.5 | +1.10% | +2.00% | 6.297 | 6.061 | -3.75% |

The steady window starts at the c-th request completion and ends at the last request submission. Tokens inside that window are estimated from stream timestamps by spreading each request's total output tokens uniformly across its streamed chunks. TPOT averages requests starting inside the steady window. AIPerf's whole-run throughput is also shown to expose the sensitivity to window and drain effects.

The PR's median steady throughput relative to the existing base-only top-32 control was +8.27%/+2.99% on 8K c=1/8 and +2.67%/+1.40% on 16K c=1/8. These comparisons have the same statistical and workload-composition limitations as the full-vocabulary comparisons.

**Statistical limits**

No statistically significant speedup is established. An exploratory two-sided exact label-permutation diagnostic, using the absolute log ratio of medians and all 20 allocations of three versus three trials, gives the following p-values:

| Workload | c | Steady throughput p | AIPerf whole-run throughput p |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 8K | 1 | 0.6 | 0.6 |
| 8K | 4 | 1.0 | 0.4 |
| 8K | 8 | 0.4 | 0.4 |
| 16K | 1 | 0.4 | 0.2 |
| 16K | 4 | 1.0 | 1.0 |
| 16K | 8 | 0.4 | 0.2 |

These are exploratory diagnostics, not confirmatory tests. Modes ran in sequential blocks, with one server startup per mode within each sweep. The three repeats therefore do not measure startup-to-startup variation, the blocks do not justify exchangeability, and duration-bounded runs consume different prompt prefixes. Several observed ranges overlap. A stronger speedup claim needs matched workloads and randomized, interleaved comparisons across independent startups.

**Acceptance length**

The strongest available comparisons use c=1 runs with matching ordered prompt sequences and identical per-request output-length vectors:

| Workload | Matched requests | Base-only AL | PR AL | Full-vocab AL | PR vs base-only | PR vs full-vocab |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 8K | 17 | 3.5631 | 3.6556 | 3.6598 | +2.60% | -0.11% |
| 16K | 15 | 3.6840 | 3.7108 | 3.7206 | +0.73% | -0.26% |

This supports AL recovery relative to base-only pruning on the sampled prompts, with the PR remaining slightly below full-vocabulary DSpark. The matched 8K subset contains one PR repeat, one full-vocab repeat and three base-only repeats. The matched 16K subset contains two PR repeats and three repeats for each control, reusing the same prompts. With only 15–17 distinct prompts, this does not establish statistical significance or generalization of the AL effect. Draft steps within a request are correlated and cannot be treated as independent prompt samples.

For completeness, the medians across all timed trials are:

| Workload | c | Base-only AL | PR AL | Full-vocab AL | PR vs full-vocab |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 8K | 1 | 3.5631 | 3.7133 | 3.7173 | -0.11% |
| 8K | 4 | n/a | 3.6313 | 3.6002 | +0.86% |
| 8K | 8 | 3.3160 | 3.4543 | 3.3869 | +1.99% |
| 16K | 1 | 3.6840 | 3.7108 | 3.7206 | -0.26% |
| 16K | 4 | n/a | 3.3768 | 3.3940 | -0.51% |
| 16K | 8 | 3.3740 | 3.3541 | 3.3251 | +0.87% |

These all-run medians should not be interpreted as matched-prompt AL improvements. For example, the 8K c=1 PR median covers 19 requests while the base-only runs cover 17. The higher-concurrency comparisons use different prompt sequences. There is no consistent demonstrated AL improvement over full-vocabulary DSpark.

The counter audit passes for all 48 included runs: `AL = 1 + accepted_tokens / num_drafts` recomputes exactly, all 384 per-position counters are complete, bounded and monotone, and their sums equal accepted-token totals. Every run records eight proposed tokens per draft. Server generation-token deltas equal client output-token totals in every run, and scrape ranges bracket the profiling phases. AL covers the whole profiling cell, including drain, rather than only the steady throughput window.

**Targeted correctness checks**

All 18 targeted tests passed, including candidate selection, reduced-vocabulary mapping and probabilistic proposal-cache agreement after CUDA graph replay. The test fixture initialized `draft_logits_num_shards=1` and `draft_logits_shard_idx=0`. Production PR code was unchanged.

End-to-end losslessness remains unverified. The eight-prompt greedy output check was inconclusive: PR versus full-vocab agreed on 5/8 and 3/8 prompts in the two sweeps, while a second full-vocab startup agreed with the first on only 4/8. [The pinned vLLM reproducibility documentation](https://github.com/mugglewei97/vllm/blob/f94d7ff8ae9ab663e4e8b08f9dd0f0326bad0b16/docs/usage/reproducibility.md) notes that default online serving does not guarantee reproducible outputs. Batch invariance was disabled for these performance measurements.

**Reproduction settings**

Use a writable shared model cache and the pinned model revisions:

```bash
export HF_HUB_CACHE=/path/to/writable/shared/cache
hf download Qwen/Qwen3-4B \
  --revision 1cfa9a7208912126459214e8b04321603b3df60c \
  --cache-dir "$HF_HUB_CACHE"
hf download AQ-MedAI/Qwen3-4B-DSpark \
  --revision 49d6beedccdb7e2500382171461cb9868c2c5fbc \
  --cache-dir "$HF_HUB_CACHE"
export TARGET=$HF_HUB_CACHE/models--Qwen--Qwen3-4B/snapshots/1cfa9a7208912126459214e8b04321603b3df60c
DRAFT=$HF_HUB_CACHE/models--AQ-MedAI--Qwen3-4B-DSpark/snapshots/49d6beedccdb7e2500382171461cb9868c2c5fbc

# Full-vocabulary DSpark
SPEC='{"method":"dspark","model":"'"$DRAFT"'","num_speculative_tokens":8}'

# PR union, or base-only with the upstream speculator.py control described above
SPEC='{"method":"dspark","model":"'"$DRAFT"'","num_speculative_tokens":8,"dspark_draft_topk":32}'

VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1 vllm serve "$TARGET" \
  --served-model-name qwen --max-model-len 32768 \
  --max-num-seqs 128 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
  --no-enable-prefix-caching --disable-uvicorn-access-log \
  --no-enable-flashinfer-autotune --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8664 --speculative-config "$SPEC"
```

The dataset revision was `nvidia/SPEED-Bench@fbd6dc64353a3153bf24252a113ebd6d2cff9dec`. Full source data were resolved using `SPEEDBench.prepare_data()` from `NVIDIA/Model-Optimizer@509acae921bad5bcb6a1fb96a8cc5ceb4fb3f6b2`, then exported to JSONL with `messages=[{"role":"user","content":turns[0]}]`. Both buckets contain 1,536 resolved prompts, with no remaining placeholders.

```bash
QUICK_ARTIFACTS=artifacts/union32-16k \
```
